utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Today is Tuesday, July 1st, 2008, and I greet our witness. I welcome Madam Prosecutors, and I welcome Mr. Seselj as well as everyone helping us. Witness, will you please stand up. Could you please give me your name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Redzep Karisik, and I was born on the 13th of July, 1952, in Sjenica in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a job at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not employed at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you unemployed or retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm unemployed and registered at the job centre. I want to retire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you already testified in front of an international court or maybe a domestic court regarding the events that occurred in the former Yugoslavia or is this the first time that you will testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, today's the first time I am testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I give you some information on what will happen now. You will be asked questions put to you by the Prosecutor. I'm sure that you have met Ms. Biersay while preparing for this hearing. Ms. Biersay has one hour and thirty minutes for questions. After that, Mr. Seselj, who is on your left, will also put questions to you, and this will be the cross-examination. The three Judges on the Bench in front of you can also intervene and ask questions at any time. Please try and be very specific in your answers. If you do not understand the meaning of a question, ask for the person putting the question to you to reformulate it. Furthermore, you have just made a solemn declaration, which means that now you are a witness of justice, you are in the hands of justice. You have undertaken, with the solemn declaration, to say the truth and only the truth. Furthermore, we will have 20-minute breaks every hour and a half so you can rest, and we also need that break in order to change the audio and videotapes. However, if at any moment you feel ill at ease, just raise your hand and I will break, I'll make a break. Also, if you have a question, just ask the Judges. I want to tell you all this so we will have a smooth hearing. Ms. Biersay, I'll greet you once again, and you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described that you were born in Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I grew up in Serbia until I was 15, in Sandzak.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where did you go after you turned 15?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Then I went all over Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you describe for us generally those areas that you went to?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Banja Luka, that's in Bosnia; Kutina in Croatia; Zajecar in Serbia, Kladovo -- I participated in work campaigns, so I'm familiar with all of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you have your education, in what area?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, I completed the building construction school in Banja Luka. I also engaged in sport, and I was busy with sports and with building construction.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where have you spent the majority of your life, in what area?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: In Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Well, do you live in Mostar now?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, I go here and there, but I'm in Mostar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For how long did you live in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Thirteen years.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thirteen, the interpreter is not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. For how many years did you live in Mostar or have you lived in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Thirty years.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what profession did you have before you described the Court you no longer have a job? What were you doing before?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I did all sorts of things, all sorts of things; building construction, I participated in youth work campaigns.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I would like for you to describe to the Trial Chamber the ethnic makeup of the Mostar area before the war started. Now, you described that you were born in Serbia. Are you Serbian or are you something else?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, at the time I was a Muslim. Now I'm a Bosniak. Before the war, we lived as one. You didn't know who was a Serb, who was a Muslim, who was a Croat, until this terrible war came along. And then when those so-called clever men caused a war, it was only then that we found out who was what.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is there a river that flows through Mostar?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, the River Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you describe to us -- you just talked about Muslims and Serbs in the Mostar area. Were there also Croats in the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for us generally where they lived in relation to the river that flowed through Mostar; right bank, left bank, and so forth?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes. For the most part, the Croats lived on the right bank of the River Neretva, and the Serbs and Muslims and Croats lived on the left bank. There were people on all sides, in Vrapcici, Bijelo Polje there were mostly Serbs and Croats and Muslims. And in Sehovina, south of Mostar, it was the same. There were mostly Muslim and Croats and down there in Buna and further on, and up there in Nevesinje, Bileca and Gacko, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could we please have 65 ter number 4273, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the map, could you describe to the Trial Chamber what military presence was in the Mostar area before the war started in 1992? Were there any military barracks in the area?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, there were military barracks in the town of Mostar. There were two, the north camp and the south camp, two barracks in town.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know if there was a military airport in or around Mostar?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: There was a military airport near Sokol. The airport was down there in Soko, Rodoc.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You've just described the military presence in Mostar before the war started. Where, specifically, did you live in Mostar before the war started?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: In the suburb of Dalejka [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were there any type of military shooting range or anything like that near your home?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there was, in Gornji Zalik, not far from the area I was familiar with. That was the first automatic shooting range in the former Yugoslavia. It was a perfect automatic shooting range.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And given the proximity of the shooting range to your home, did you have any opportunities to interact with the JNA soldiers who would come there?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, with the officers and the soldiers, the privates, because I lived nearby, nearby the shooting range, about 100 or 200 metres away from it. There were five soldiers working there to maintain the shooting range.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you do compulsory military service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in 1970 and 1971, in Tito's Guard in Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you just described that you were familiar with the types of JNA soldiers who would come to the shooting range. Were you also familiar with the types of JNA soldiers who would be in and around town, connected to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, I knew the four soldiers employed on maintaining the shooting range because there was a playing field there and we would -- two were from Novi Sad, one was from Belgrade, and the fourth was from Drvar. They were active-duty soldiers. They served for 18 months. Later on, it was reduced to 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to now direct your attention to approximately April of 1992. Around that time, did you notice any JNA reservists coming into the area?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, they did come.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what did they look like? Did they look like the JNA soldiers that you were already familiar with?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: They looked like JNA soldiers by their uniform, but not by their behaviour. And what they looked like, they had long beards and long hair, and they weren't as disciplined as the regular soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you say they weren't as disciplined as the regular soldiers, could you describe to the Trial Chamber what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, what I mean is the following: Real soldiers had their hair cut and they were polite and well-behaved. These men didn't have any commanders. They obeyed no one. They did whatever they wanted, these reservists.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described that they had the long beards and hair. Did they seem different to you in any other way; for example, through their accents?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, they each spoke their own -- in their own accent. I can tell what people in Serbia speak like, talk like. I can speak that dialect, and so I could tell.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did all of these JNA reservists have the Serbian dialect or were there different kinds of dialects spoken by them?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Different.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. This sort of question can't be put. It's not a Serbian dialect, it's an Ekavian dialect. The Serbs speak Ekavian and Ijekavian, so you can't call the Ekavian dialect the Serbian dialect. And the Muslims in Sandzak also speak the Ekavian dialect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You already said this. Ms. Biersay, please take what Mr. Seselj said into account.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness might complete that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in Tito's time, some people called you "Comrade," other people called you "Sir." I think that the people spoke every dialect. Serbia speak Ekavian, Montenegro, Bosnia. That's not just one nation. All people, whoever lived in Serbia, spoke Ekavian. I can't say that Serbs and Muslims did not speak Ekavian or Roma. They all spoke the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Karisik, where were these JNA reservists that you describe? Where were they stationed, as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: The south camp and the north camp and Vrapcici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there's a small detail that emerged. I know we've seen a good number of witnesses, but I've never asked them this question. Obviously, you're someone who travelled a lot in Serbia, you know Serbia. So these reservists who came in town and who had beards, before these events and before the war, could you tell us whether in Serbia men were used to wear beards, it was quite commonplace, and to see someone with a big beard was very normal? Could you tell us whether those people who came with those long beards came into Mostar but were very different from the people you were used to seeing before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer your question. I used to wear a beard, myself. It was this long [indicates]. But there was preparation going on for that war, the war was being prepared, and there were people who didn't cut their hair or shave, and they had hair down to here [indicates]. And the way they behaved and everything. If I wear a beard, okay, but I won't be unkempt; I won't be dirty. I used to wear a beard, too, even though I was a sportsman and participated in youth work drives, I still wore a beard. But I wasn't preparing for war, because in those reserves, those reservists who came from Serbia, there were also Muslims in the reserves, and as soon as they saw them coming, they fled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could I clarify something you just said? You said that when they saw them coming, they fled. Who fled?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: If I had a house, I would have run away. If I had somewhere to run to, I would have run.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What would you be running away from? What were people running away from?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, they were running because they were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what were they afraid of?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: They were afraid because they saw what was happening in Croatia. There was a war first in Slovenia, then in Croatia, and then it came to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You just described the arrival of JNA reservists. Was there another wave of military-type people that came after the JNA reservists?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: They came and went. You didn't know who was who, who was doing what. Everybody wanted to be in command. Everybody wanted to have their say. And whoever was weaker fled from whoever was stronger.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to the JNA soldiers that you got to know because they were coming to the shooting range next to your house. Did you ever talk to them about who these different military people were who were coming into the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, I've forgotten their names. It was a long time ago, 16 or 17 years ago, and I'm sorry. Well, I'd like to see them again today, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What did they tell you about the people -- the reservists and the JNA soldiers and the other people who were coming into Mostar? What did the JNA soldiers that you knew say about those people?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: They said, "It's just the Territorial Defence that's come here. There will be some kind of exercise and it will all be over in a week. It's not going to last long." That's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did that happen or did something else happen?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Then the worst happened. Somebody managed to set -- to start a fire. They put a cistern in front of the building and then set fire to the thing, and then it all blew up.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether or not these JNA reservists and others were stationed in places like Bileca, Trebinje, Nevesinje; do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, there is information, but what kind of information, the active-duty army withdrew when the order came. The real army withdrew to Serbia. That was the order, and the real army withdrew. Now, who joined the reservists and who stayed on, they stayed on. They had weapons, military weapons. They had everything the army left behind. It's just that the army took away light weapons. Everything else remained, because the active-duty soldiers withdrew when the order came for them to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know when they withdrew?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber what the JNA soldiers said about Seseljevci and Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, until they begin doing evil things, there wasn't so much of that. But as soon as they started doing evil things, then, yes, that's what happened. There were all sorts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say "all sorts," all sorts of what?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: All sorts; rape, slaughter, killings, everything. But until the killing started and -- well, life was normal, you live normally. But as soon as all that started, all kinds of things started, well, then it was just chaos.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I don't want to focus on what happened as far as crimes yet. What I'd like you to do is to describe for the Trial Chamber what military units or formations were present in Mostar after April 1992.

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: When the army withdrew, the real army, the reservists remained. And afterwards, those people who joined up with them, the paramilitary units who nobody commanded. Everybody wanted to have his own, his own company to go and fight, loot, kill.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What paramilitary units were present in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Seselj's men, I don't know who commanded them or who was their vojvoda.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I don't know who was their vojvoda, but somebody fought to be a vojvoda. Now, who the vojvoda was and who gave orders, you, Comrade, know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Karisik, because we have the time that the Trial Chamber just discussed, you have to listen very carefully to my questions and answer just the question so that we can move forward in an efficient manner. Okay?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, I can go on talking for a whole night and a whole day if you'll let me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I know, but we only have 90 minutes and we have to be very efficient. So my question --

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, you can extend the time, then, and then we can go on, continue on and on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid we can't. So my question to you is : In addition to the Seselj's men that you described, were there other military formations or units who were present in the area of Mostar, in and around the time period that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: This is what -- who was there: The Green Berets, as they were called, the Seselj's men as they were called, Chetniks, as they called them, the White Eagles, and who knows what else, what other kind of soldiers. And whatever kind of army turned up like that, I would flee, I would have fled. You didn't know who anybody belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you have your family members leave the area of Mostar because of your concerns?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: A colleague of mine, a Croat, suggested that I do that, and I prepared my -- I got my wife and children ready, and he drove them away. I couldn't go, but he drove them away.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And why couldn't you go? Why did you stay?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I couldn't go. I had things to attend to for the company. I had my duties there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. What company were you working for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vranica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what kind of company was it? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: A construction firm.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At some point, did it happen that you were forced to work collecting garbage in and around the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber how that happened?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: We were -- we were held for two and a half months in Zalik, Upper Zalik, Lower Zalik, and north camp part of town. There was Matkovici, and we were there in a collection centre, and from there we would go and clean garbage and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What collection centre were you in?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Some of them were in the shelters. In Zalik, there are two shelters. And some of us went to some houses or went home, but then we had to report from our homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Let's take one step back for a minute. You described to the Trial Chamber that at some point, you were -- you were working with this company that you described; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And at the same time, you described that people eventually made their way to these shelters. Could you describe why people were going to shelters in the first place?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, that was sort of safest for them. They were safest there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What were they trying to be safe from? What were they afraid of?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: They were afraid. When the others started looting the houses, they were frightened that they would kill them in the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In addition to looting, was there any type of gunshots heard or were there any kind of shellings in and around the area?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, shells were falling from the hills all over, on the left bank and on the right bank too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And were those things going on at the time people decided to go into shelters?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At some point, did the Serb forces take over the left bank of the River Neretva?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: They took control of the left bank straight away, while the real army was still there, the JNA. That side was taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And on what side were the shelters? Were they on the left bank or on the right bank?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: The left bank.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where did you live, on the right bank or the left bank?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: The left bank.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After the left bank of the Neretva area of Mostar was taken over by Serb forces, is that when you had to do forced labour?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, that's when I went.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who told you that you had to do this kind of work?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Matkovic said, the one that was in Zalik. He had the warehouse and everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who is he?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: He was a Serb, and he was the main man down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How many people were told that they had to do work that was not their choice? Do you know, approximately?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, sometimes there were 50, sometimes 60, sometimes 40, depending on who was able to come. Some people weren't healthy, they were ill, so they stayed home.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber what kind of work you were forced to do?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: All kinds of work. We cleaned the garbage, took it away; washed the streets; loaded up construction materials, equipment; offloaded, loaded up, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you did this kind of work, was there anyone guarding you?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes. Two soldiers were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of the people who guarded you while you were forced to do this kind of work?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I've forgotten their names, but they didn't touch us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you were doing this forced work, was there still fighting going on?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, there was shooting up in the hills, but it was quiet in town.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who is Milan Skoro?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Milan Skoro was a former policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did he do in connection to your forced work that you had to do?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: He issued orders, telling us where and what we should do. He would say, "Go there, go over there."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: While you were doing this forced labour, did you see any of the units that you talked about; Seseljevci, or Red Berets, or any other units like that?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: There were, but you couldn't distinguish who was who. Some had cowboy hats, others had caps. You couldn't really tell who was who: Who was commanding people over here and people over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described people going into these shelters. You said there were two shelters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when people started going into the shelters?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Straight away from the 2nd of April, when the water tank exploded. Not two days went by.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where is this water tank that you just talked about?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Right up the wall by the barracks, not two metres away in north camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Approximately how many people would go into these shelters or into the specific shelter that you're talking about, how many people?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: There were women and children and men, and 500, 600 in a shelter. Gornji Zalik, Donji Zalik, Upper and Lower Zalik, part of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And am I correct in saying that by that, you mean that they came from all the areas around the barracks?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: The whole area, Zalik, Gornji Zalik, Donji Zalik, and all the settlements 'round about when the shelters were made.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When people first started going into the shelters, were there non-Serbs as well as Serbs?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: There were Serbs, and Croats, and Muslims, gypsies, anybody who didn't want to go to war.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did that change after a while? Were there only non-Serbs who were staying inside the shelter?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I was just there for a night in that shelter, and I didn't go anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I was at home, the four of us in houses. We slept around in houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say "the four of us," are you talking about family members or other neighbours?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: No, neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After the water tower you described was blown up, were you taken into custody for interrogation at the north camp?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is completely out of order. Which water tank was blown up? A tank truck was brought to north camp, an explosive was planted there, and then the tank truck was blown up, and otherwise the Prosecutor is posing increasingly leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this water tank which exploded, which is mentioned in the Prosecution's submissions and in the Prosecution's brief, did somebody put an explosive there? What actually happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't a water tower. There was water or fuel, petrol. We're not talking about a water tower or a water truck. I wasn't there to fill it up with explosives or planting explosives there. If it was positioned there, it might have been positioned -- well, explosives or shells or petrol, fuel, might have been put in there, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, it's a water tank, it's not a fuel tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what kind of tank it was. Let me put myself right. It might have been for water. It might have been for petrol. It might have been for fuel. It might have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you were taken to the north camp for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Who interrogated you there?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I was interrogated by the army, the real army, 14 of us, but then they let us go. We spent a night there. They asked who was shooting at the army. I didn't know who was shooting. I wasn't shooting. If I was shooting -- if I were shooting, I would have been where the shooting was going on. So don't say I'm a Zenga when I'm not a Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know anyone with the last name Savic?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: There's a Savic from Rastani, but I don't know his first name. All I know is that that's his surname, Savic. He took us to north camp. We spent the night there. They interrogated us and then they left us go. They sent two to Bileca and they let the rest of us go.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How many of you were taken to north camp for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Fourteen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat that again?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Fourteen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: While you were at the north camp, were you sitting in a chair, were you laying down on a bed?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: We weren't given anything. We could just stand like this [indicates] on our knees, with our hands behind our backs, tilted to the side. You couldn't even stand straight.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At some point, now directing your attention to June of 1992, did you try to leave by going through the town Potoci?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I started to flee from there, I couldn't take it anymore, towards Jablanica and then, well, to Bijelo Polje, where they captured the four of us with a Land Rover, and I recognised Mladin Kandic. He was a former policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you recognise anybody else?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't recognise anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who were the others that you were travelling with or trying to escape with?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Karisik, one minute. Let me ask you -- what are you looking at? Are you looking at a statement that you provided to the --

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm looking at Enes Mezet, Omer Hasic and his wife. The four of us started to flee, we started to escape.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you were taken by the people that you just mentioned, including this Kandic, is that correct, where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: They took me 19 kilometres away from Mostar towards the north, Rakovac, the post.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say "post," what do you mean? Is it a post office?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, post office, the PTT, which was part of the settlement there. That's where the post office was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And while you were there with the others, were other people brought in as well as prisoners?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: They brought in two more men from Podvelezje. They caught them at Rujiste, and they shut them up in a WC.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what is Podvelezje?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Podvelezje is a settlement with inhabitants. Five or six thousand inhabitants it had.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you at any point while you were being held at the post office ask Mandzic to let you go?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Since I knew him, I said to him, "Let me go. I'm gone to look for my wife and children." I lied to him just to make him release me. He said, "A bullet to your head rather than let you go." "But why?" He kept quiet.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear a part of what the witness said after he said "my wife and child," that he had gone looking for them and he lied.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After you asked to let them go, what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Nothing. He said, "A bullet to your head rather than let you go."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How many days did you spend at the post office, approximately?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Three days and three nights.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where were you taken next?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: To Sutina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what is in Sutina?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: That's where the cemetery is, the municipal cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, before us is the map, 65 ter number 4273, which depicts, Konjic, Mostar and Nevesinje and some other areas. We'd move for the admission of the map at this time before I proceed to another map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: For what purpose? What is it going to show us?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the purpose of showing us this map?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: This map before the Court is to orient the Court with respect to Mostar and the surrounding villages, as described by the witness, and it includes Vrapcici, which he will address, and the location of Nevesinje, with respect to Mostar as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I suggest you wait to seek admission until the witness has provided his information onto the map, because a bare map is worth nothing, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, directing your attention to the map before you that's on your screen --

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I can see the map very well. It's like this: Let me explain to the Trial Chamber. Sutina, that's where -- well, there's a pit there. Twenty-two were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One minute, please. One minute, please. Could you show the Court, by touching the screen, the River Neretva that flows through Mostar?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I can do that. Here [indicates], right by Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is it possible for him to make a mark so we can capture an annotation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I think there's no point in the witness marking the River Neretva, which can be clearly seen. It's best if you show us where Sutina is and where Uborak is and mark that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's five or ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could we now move to 65 ter number 2863, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, does that mean that the Prosecutor has desisted from tendering this document? What's most important is -- this map is to see where Sutina is, because to be quite honest, I don't know where Sutina and Uborak are, and the witness would show us that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on the map before you, do you see Sutina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It just says "Vrapcici," here. It just says "Vrapcici." It doesn't say Sutina. It doesn't say Uborak either. Uborak is up there where the military barracks is where there was a rubbish dump next to the barracks. It doesn't say Uborak it just says garbage dump is. It doesn't say "Uborak" here. It just says "Vrapcici," all of Bijelo Polje, all of Vrapcici. There isn't that place marked here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you well, Vrapcici -- Sutina is next to Vrapcici.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could interrupt for a moment, if we could have 65 ter number 2863, I think this would assist us all. The first purpose of the map was to give us an overall geographical orientation for the Court. We're now going to zoom into the specific area, which is 65 ter number 2863. It's a pretty dense file, so it's taking some time to load. So while it's being loaded:

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mr. Karisik, could you describe for the Trial Chamber what happened when you got to Sutina, the Sutina cemetery?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Where the administration of the cemetery was, there was a team questioning people. And when Kandic got there to be questioned, the people in there said, "They're not for here. Take them to Vrapcici."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And do you remember the name of the person who said, "They're not for here. Take them to Vrapcici"?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I didn't go inside. I don't know who was there or how many people there were inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you -- where were you taken after they took you from the Sutina cemetery?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Along the main road, some 600 or 700 metres down the road, to the stadium in Vrapcici, the changing rooms; locker room, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How big was the locker room where you were taken?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, the locker room, I didn't measure it, but it was less than 30 square metres, all of it together.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you arrived at the locker room and they took you inside, were there already people inside the locker room?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: There were 37 men there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were there any women there?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, there were women and children too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For how long were you kept in the Vrapcici stadium's locker room?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Six days and six nights.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And during those six days and six nights, did the number 37 change of the people who were kept in that locker room?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, they brought in people every day and every night.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how large a number was there of people in the locker room?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Ninety, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: While you were there, did you meet anyone who had been there longer than you had been there?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Omer Brekalo from Kuti Livce.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How long did he say he had been kept in that locker room?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Twenty days.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the guards who were bringing people in, into the locker room?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I only recognised [indiscernible] from Nevesinje. His name was Mico Bunjas. He used to work with me in Vranica for 15 years. I didn't know his real name. They called him Gunjar, but his name was Misa Vucic. I didn't even know his real name. We called him Gunjar. He didn't even see me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber what it felt like to be in that locker room with 89 other people in June? How did it feel?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, I longed for death, because before I arrived, 50 Croats were taken to Bileca, and we thought they would kill us all. We thought they wouldn't take us to Bileca to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, "I expected to die."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: While you were kept prisoner in the Vrapcici locker room with these other 89 people, were you given food, water?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Those six days? Only once. On the fourth day when I went to Podvelezje, I drank and had my fill.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After you'd left the locker room?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you say that you drank water, but only after four days. I'm a bit surprised. Are you absolutely sure that you could only get a drink once and that you had to stay four days without anything to drink?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm sure, only once, only once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood you well, you drank once in four days and you ate once in six days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. You understood me well, and I said it right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe to the Trial Chamber how you were finally taken out of the Vrapcici locker room? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: It was nighttime, about 10.00, 10.30 p.m. A white van stopped in front of the door. A bearded man got out. He had a helmet on. He wore a uniform. And he said, "You are going to another place." And we thought, well, where are we going. There were five or six of us who were there together, and he said, "You're going somewhere else." And we got into the van. Five or six of us whom I know got on, and then others got on as well, 15 or 20, as many as could be packed into the van.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where were you in the van; were you in the back or the front?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: At the front.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So by "front," you mean the part closer to the driver?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, but there was a partition between us and the driver. We had no contact with the driver.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what happened next after everyone was crammed into that van?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: The van started. We didn't know where we were going. It wasn't an asphalt road, it was a dirt road; after some ten minutes, that is. First there was this asphalt and then this dirt road or macadam. And then the van stopped. The man opened the door, and the people at the end started getting out. And as they were getting out, this man started shooting them down with bursts of fire. I remember well one who -- one prisoner who got out said, "Dragan, we know each other. We've known each other for 30 years." And he just shot him down. So whoever got out of the van, I don't know how many there were, and I remained. Are there more? "Yes, get out." But I couldn't stand up because my legs were shaking, I couldn't stand up, so I said, "I can't get up. Kill me here in the van." Then he swore at my Ustasha mother. He slammed the door shut and he said, "We'll kill you in another way." And he took me back to Sutina, where I had been first. The van pulled up. He said, "Get out." But I couldn't stand up. I crawled out on my knees. There were two of them with beards and helmets. It was night. I didn't know them. And the one who tied me up, he spoke Ekavian, Serbian, the way I speak, and that's how I know he was from Serbia, by his speech. He used the word "Bre," he swore at my Ustasha mother, but I am no Ustasha and no Zenga. I crawled out on my hands and knees, and I was beaten. He handcuffed me to the radiator and left. I said, "Why are you handcuffing me? You're going to lock the door anyway." And then he hit me again and left. I don't know for how long I stayed there handcuffed to that radiator. He switched the engine on and left in the van. I was handcuffed by one hand. I'm sorry, I didn't bring the handcuffs here. I've kept them as a souvenir, and I wish I'd brought them here to show you. I managed to wrench it off and escape through the window. And it was five days later that I was able to eat and drink my fill.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How long did it take you to wrench out of the handcuffs?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: About ten minutes. I was fit and strong.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how did you do it, how did you get out of the handcuffs?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I had a little pen knife, so I blocked something so it wouldn't turn, and then I managed to break one of the links in the chain. So one end of the handcuffs remained on the radiator and the other end on my hand, on my arm, but I managed to break the chain.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where did you go after you were able to break out of the handcuffs?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Through the window, through the cemetery, up the hill, and then to Podvelezje.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you left, did you have the part of the handcuffs still around your wrist?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, until the next day. They only took it off when I got up there. A policeman called Zajko used a needle to take it off. He unlocked it with a needle in five seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: After you escaped from the Sutina cemetery, where did you ultimately go after the handcuffs were taken off? Where did you end up?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I went down to Mostar when the BH Army liberated Podvelezje. That's when I went down to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to direct your attention to the map that's before you, which is 65 ter number 2863. Could you, using --

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Starting at the bottom --

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Sutina, Vrapcici stadium, Vrapcici up there, Uborak. It's marked up there, so now you can tell everything, where everything is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: The markings that are on this map, are they accurate? Is that where Uborak is; is that where Vrapcici stadium is?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, it's marked here, "Uborak," "Vrapcici," the stadium, "Sutina" down there, and "North camp" and "Zalik."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And where the north camp --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, you're going to ask for this map be admitted, so maybe you could ask the witness to place a "1" next to Uborak," a "2" next to the stadium, a "3" next to Sutina, a "4" next to the north camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you please put a "1" the area Uborak? If you put a "1." You can actually use it to write on the screen. It's like a pen.

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Uborak [marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you please put a "2" next to the Vrapcici stadium?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Vrapcici stadium [marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And then a "3" next to Sutina?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And a "4" next to the north camp?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How long would it take to drive from Uborak down to the north camp?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, it depends on whether you use the main road. Five minutes, five minutes. If you use the dirt road -- there may be an asphalt road through Vrapcici here, so if you don't go down there towards the Neretva but use the asphalt road, then it's 10 minutes or 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you were being -- when the people in the van were being taken out and shot, did you know where you were at that time?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when is it that you learned that -- you learned where the location of that shooting was?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I only learned that when I arrived in Sutina, when I was tied up. That's when I found out.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: How did you find out?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Because my company had built the city cemetery and the administration building and everything. I had worked on the construction.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you knew, when you were in Sutina. How did you later find out that you had been taken to the Uborak location?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I learned that only later on, when the mass grave was found, when north camp was liberated, and Vrapcici and Bijelo Polje. I identified 22 persons in Sutina and 88 from Uborak.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we would move for the annotated version of 2863 as well as the original, so we'd seek the admission of both versions of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Madam Registrar, could we have a number for the annotated mark -- the annotated map and another number for the more general map, number 4273.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The annotated map will become Exhibit P479, and the original map will become Exhibit P480, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, Madam Registrar, if we could now have 65 ter number 7248, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise this list that's before you?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who do you recognise those people to be? Who are they?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: They were all with me in Vrapcici. They were killed at Uborak.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, we'd move for the admission of 65 ter number 7248, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can we have a number for this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit P481, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So just to be clear, these people you recognise as people who were with you in the Vrapcici locker room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You also described that you participated in the exhumation of the mass grave, and where was that mass grave, the Uborak-related one? Where was that mass grave in Uborak? Could you describe it?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: The rubbish dump 88 in Sutina, next to the River Neretva, 22. That was a separate mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: With respect to the 88 who were found at the Uborak dump -- it's a dump, that's how you describe it? It's a rubbish dump; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you identify other people, as well as the names that we just saw on this exhibit? There were other people that you knew; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did you participate in the identification of those other bodies as well?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Were you present for the actual exhumation, the bodies that were being dug up? Were you present for that part or did you just see the bodies after they were taken out?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I went from Sutina to Uborak and from Uborak by car to Sutina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In addition to the -- could we go back to the previous exhibit, please. I believe it's P481. These 18 people on this list, do you know the ethnicity of any of them?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: There were Croats here, Marko Mihalj. I identified him by his shoes and his socks, because he couldn't walk. I called his son to see whether that was his father. I recognised him by his shoes and his socks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you described a Croat. Do you know the ethnicity of the other people on that list?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: They were all Muslims, now Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be a good time for a pause?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's have a break. According to our computations, I think you have 18 minutes left. We are now going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, you have the floor. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed our hearing, and Ms. Biersay has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just by way of clarification, the Prosecution had asked for the admission of the original 65 ter number 2863, with the annotation. That was the second one that had the local places marked. And we'd also moved for the admission of the first one, the orienting one, with Mostar and Nevesinje, which is 65 ter number 4273.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We already have two exhibit numbers. This has been done already, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And with respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, as far as Exhibit number 2863 is concerned, you would like the map to be tendered; in other words, the annotated? Which do you wish to tender into evidence, the map that has been marked or the one that hasn't been marked?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: We'd like to have both, Your Honour, as an A/B grouping if the Court prefers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Mics, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, the Trial Chamber has just deliberated on the matter and holds that the mark -- the map that has been marked is enough. There is no need to tender into evidence a map that has not been marked. We already have an exhibit number for this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, then for clarification, map 2863, with the witness's annotations, is Exhibit P479, and the first map bearing 65 ter 4273 is Exhibit P480. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. And at this time, Your Honour, the Prosecution would end its examination-in-chief, and to the extent there's any redirect permitted, we would ask for the reserve time to be used then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, just some recommendations before the cross-examination starts, which can be a delicate moment. You will have to answer the questions that will be put to you by Mr. Seselj. Please remain calm and answer the questions. Sometimes you may not like the questions, but the accused is entitled to ask any question he likes. So please stay calm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have the right to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And wait for him to finish his question before you answer. Count until five. Since you are going to be speaking the same language, the interpreters have to have enough time to translate what you are saying. So when he puts a question, count until five and then answer. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I first have to say that telephone wasn't working this morning or the fax machine. So there were some attempts to send me some documents via fax, but that was unsuccessful because the machine just gobbled up whole sentences. I just wanted to draw your attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Karisik, I think there is no reason for you to be nervous, although the Judges brought that to your attention and cautioned you, because I think you testified truthfully, and within the framework of what you told to us, I see nothing that I would have to challenge especially. So I would like to start off by asking you a question outside the circle incorporated into the Prosecution questions. The representative of the OTP started from April 1992, but since you lived in Mostar, you should know that the conflicts between the JNA and the Croatian military formations started already in September 1991 in Mostar. Right?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I'm not a military analyst for me to know any of these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you were present. You know of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, I did follow it. They are things that I follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina broke up, before the Serbs and the Muslims and the before the proclamation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we're talking about September 1991; right? You can't remember?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I can't remember. As I say, I'm not a politician. I don't deal with politics, nor am I interested in politics. I'm just sorry that the conflict broke out in the first place. I'm very sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In April 1992, the proclamation of independence for Bosnia-Herzegovina came. The Western powers proclaimed that, and in April the war broke out between the Serbs and Muslims, and there was no war before that. So for a full seven months, September, October, November, December, January, February, March, and the beginning of April, for a full seven months it was exclusively a conflict between the JNA and the Croatian paramilitary forces in the Mostar area; right?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: It was all over the place, on the whole territory, and it incorporated Bosnia too, that part of Croatia and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Wherever there was a high concentration of Croats, there were conflicts; right?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: No. Wherever you Serbs wanted to have your republic, like you got it in Bosnia, and you would have got Knin, too, had you gone on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's not have any philosophical questions here or deal in politics. Let's just look at the facts. The conflict between the JNA and Croatian paramilitaries lasted for a full seven months, right, before April 1992; isn't that right? And there was shooting in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: He has already posed this question to the witness. The witness has said, "I don't know. I'm not a politician. I don't remember." And he's asked the question at least three times now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please listen to what I'm about to say. Mr. Seselj has put a question to you. This question is important, because the events that occurred in April 1992, which relate to the Serbs, on the one hand, and the Croats and the Muslims, on the other hand, taken like that one has the feeling that the problems began to arise in April. But in light of Mr. Seselj's question, purportedly there were paramilitary formations that were Croatian in Mostar. Did you know that, did you not know that? And if Croatian paramilitary forces were present, there may have been a confrontation between these Croatian paramilitary forces in Mostar and the Serbs before April 1992. What can you tell us about this? Do you know about this or don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I can't really say. As to conflicts, whether there were any before that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to put you right. It was a conflict between the JNA and the Croatian paramilitary forces, not a conflict between the Serbs and Croats, because in the JNA you had Muslims too; not in large numbers, because a portion of them failed to respond to the mobilisation call, but there were quite a lot of them. And it was still officially the JNA as the sole military force of Yugoslavia of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I object to Mr. Seselj testifying. He should simply put the question to the witness and have the witness respond. But these types of explanations amount to testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, first of all, I have not made a mistake. On line 19, page 37, I mentioned the Croatian paramilitary forces. This is what I said. I did not say anything else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you said, Mr. President, that they were in conflict with the Serbs, and that's where you corrected what I said erroneously. I said "with the JNA," but you turned the "JNA" into "Serbia." You said "Serbia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I find it strange, since you lived in Mostar, that you didn't know about this conflict between the JNA and the Croatian paramilitaries. Now, in the autumn of 1991, Mostar was, in actual fact, divided along the Neretva River, on the one side, on the left bank, it was the JNA that was in control, and the Croatian paramilitaries controlled the right bank?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I was a construction worker and I was working on site. I didn't really live in Mostar. I was on site.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, in the autumn of 1991, were you working in the field?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I was in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And where did you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers slow down and make pauses between question and answer. It's impossible to follow at this speed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. You are going too fast, both of you, and the interpreters can't keep track. Please go more slowly, speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you returned before the new year, the conflict between the JNA and Croatian paramilitaries was still going on, although there was a ceasefire, but Mostar was, to all intents and purposes, divided, so you couldn't go to whichever part of Mostar you wanted freely?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: The JNA took the left side and you couldn't go anymore, you couldn't cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the right side was held by the Croatian paramilitaries; right? And the Muslims still did not involve themselves in the conflict, when you came back from Germany just before the new year; right?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: You can come and go. You could go to Germany and to Bosnia and come back to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But since you lived on the eastern bank of the Neretva River, you couldn't cross over to the western bank, could you?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I came from the right bank to the left bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Nicely, I came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the JNA have control of the bridges?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the other side, did you have the Croatian paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: There was nobody except soldiers. It was only the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And who had control of West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: You had soldiers on whom the JNA to the last withdrawal --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Whom [as interpreted] is the hill above Mostar?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, but the right bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, a large hill where the JNA was until its withdrawal in 1992?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But who controlled the western part of town? There was no JNA down there, was there?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: That's where the main hospital was. By the old hospital, the military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Just a moment. Who held control of the largest portion of West Mostar when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: It was under the control of the civilian -- well, the civilians that controlled it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What army controlled it?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Army? There was no army on that side. You didn't have to ask yourself who was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, who went to war against the JNA, then? Who did -- who fought against the JNA, then?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: The reservists. The reservists were the ones that caused all the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's leave problems aside for a moment. I know what you said about problems. But on the one side we had the JNA with its reservists, with its reserve force, its regular troops and reserve force, and who was on the opposite side, the opposing side?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: You have Bosnia. Bosnia had its army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1991, when you came back from Germany, before it was recognised.

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: All you had was the JNA and the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, who was the adversary, who was opposed to them then?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: They wanted to rule themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: This is asking, in a different format, the same question that seven to ten minutes ago the witness answered, which is he did not -- does not know about Croatian paramilitaries being in conflict with the JNA in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have answered, but we are a little bit surprised by your answer, and I shall tell you why. According to what I understand, you went to work in Germany and you came back before the end of the year 1991. You have East Mostar and West Mostar. In West Mostar, were there any military present? Did you see any at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no paramilitaries over there then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you quite sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certain, sure and certain, except on the left side the reservists, that was the TO, Territorial Defence. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And during this period at the end of 1991, January, February, March 1992, was there no fighting that pitched the JNA against those people in West Mostar, according to what you know? Was there any fighting or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't find any combat going on because Vance's plan was already in force, which established a truce between Croatia and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, right, so that the fighting stopped in Herzegovina too; right?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Owen's plan was not adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That wasn't Owen's plan, that was Vance's plan.

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. They drew maps here and there, but none of it came into being.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Since you didn't see any military forces on the West Bank of Mostar, I'm not going to insist upon that anymore. Now, what do you understand by the term "Seselj's men," "Seseljevci"?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: "Seselj's men"? Well, soldiers who had command, that is, Seselj's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: An army commanded by Seselj?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, if you were the commander, that's how they got their name. Somebody who has an army, it's his army. If you had command there, who else's army would it be there? Were there any other Seseljs?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever see this army of Seselj's?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I just saw the -- I heard the soldiers with their dialect and knew that they were from Serbia, and they called them "Seselj's men."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that you heard other people refer to them as being Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you heard them speaking Ekavian?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, they're speaking the same way as I'm speaking now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that's all, is it? You know nothing more that could identify them in any way?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I wasn't with them, so how could I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, when you were in Vrapcici and Sutina, did you see Seselj's men over there, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: I was incarcerated, so from inside I couldn't see who was outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. We'll move a little faster now, I hope. On the 2nd of April, there was this explosion in front of north camp barracks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And a tank full of explosives was brought in with some metal parts, who knows what, a tank truck, and it exploded in front of the barracks; right?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what was in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. But the explosion took place, and it destroyed the barracks, to a large extent; right?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: It destroyed the wall and the surrounding parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And some of the dormitories were destroyed, et cetera, things like that; right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Well, there was something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was, right. The whole wall to the building toppled down and you could see the inside of the building, the dormitories and so on?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: There were storehouses, storage space, dormitories, but I couldn't see all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were arrested for the first time when the army conducted an investigation as to who planted the explosive?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was in April. They held you for a month and they released you. They had two Croatian suspects, and they sent them to Bileca, to the military prison there, is that right, two of them?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they let the rest go?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes, and 12 of us remained.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're going too fast. Mr. Seselj, please go more slowly, because the interpreters are having a hard time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So of the 14 people, two were suspects. After making their statements, they went to prison, and 12 persons were released. Did the soldiers beat you while they were interrogating you?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who beat you?

utterances.speaker: REDZEP KARISIK
